name: Hsiung Feng II anti-ship missile
operator: Republic of China (Taiwan) Navy & coastal defence
overview_md:
The Hsiung Feng II ("Brave Wind II") is Taiwan's indigenous subsonic anti-ship cruise missile — the workhorse anti-ship weapon of the Republic of China Navy and a core element of the island's sea-denial strategy against a Chinese amphibious invasion. Developed by NCSIST and in service since the 1990s, it arms Taiwan's frigates, missile boats and coastal-defence batteries.

A sea-skimming, turbojet-powered missile in the class of the U.S. Harpoon, the Hsiung Feng II flies low over the water to a range of roughly 150–250 km and uses a combination of active radar and imaging-infrared seekers to find and strike ships even in cluttered, jamming-rich coastal waters. A land-attack derivative, the Hsiung Feng IIE, extends Taiwan's reach against targets on the Chinese mainland with a range reported in the hundreds of kilometres.

For an analyst, the Hsiung Feng II embodies Taiwan's "porcupine" strategy: large numbers of mobile, concealable anti-ship missiles designed to make a cross-strait invasion fleet pay a prohibitive price. Cheaper and more numerous than its supersonic sibling the Hsiung Feng III, it provides the volume of fire — from ships and from hidden coastal launchers — that would help contest the narrow, crowded waters of the Taiwan Strait in the opening phase of any conflict.

additional.launch_platforms: Frigates, missile boats, coastal batteries, aircraft

builder: National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST)

combat_history.event: No combat use; backbone anti-ship missile of the ROC Navy and coastal defence.

modernization.description: Increased production and mobile coastal deployment.
modernization.impact: Multiplies the anti-ship fires available to contest an invasion.

vulnerabilities.description: Slower than supersonic missiles, giving defences more reaction time.
vulnerabilities.context: Modern fleet air defence can engage it.

vulnerabilities.description: Coastal targeting infrastructure is itself a target.

operational_patterns.typical_deployment: Anti-ship sea denial from frigates, missile boats and concealed coastal batteries in the Taiwan Strait.
operational_patterns.typical_task_group: ROC Navy combatants and coastal-defence missile groups.

peer_comparisons.key_differences: The HF-3 is the faster supersonic 'carrier killer'; the HF-2 provides cheaper, more numerous subsonic volume.
Comparable subsonic anti-ship missile; Taiwan operates both Harpoon and the indigenous HF-2.
The threat fleet's anti-ship missile; the HF-2 is what would strike that fleet.
peer_comparisons.video_angle: The missile duel in the strait.

doctrine.role: Indigenous subsonic anti-ship cruise missile — the workhorse of Taiwan's sea denial.
doctrine.employment: Sea-skimming attack from ships, missile boats and concealed coastal batteries against an invasion fleet.
doctrine.design_philosophy: Numerous, affordable, mobile anti-ship fires — the 'porcupine' approach.
doctrine.threat_context: Volume fire to make a cross-strait amphibious assault prohibitively costly.
doctrine.comparison_frame: Read with the supersonic HF-3 and against the Harpoon and China's YJ-18.
